correctness.rationale: For each complete mapping, the row maps p_i and output-column maps q_j are independent permutations, giving a bijection to S_b^a times S_a^b. The fixed-set probability is exactly a product of inverse falling factorials; expanding t^F gives the exact distribution for all a,b>=1. Three distinct ordered-pair classes give variance 1+1/(ab) for a,b>=2, with separately verified one-side-size-one boundaries. For each fixed k, uniform falling-factorial expansion gives factorial moment tending to 1 as min(a,b)->infinity, proving Poisson(1) convergence by moment determinacy. The standalone checker independently tests the actual semigroup multiplication and full fixed-point histograms on four small grids; the 3x3 formula is checked separately.

originality.rationale: The source paper arXiv:2608.25092v1 establishes existence classifications for Rees matrix semigroups, enumerates complete mappings of combinatorial Brandt semigroups using Latin squares in Section 6.1, and establishes bands rigidity results in Section 12, but explicitly poses cycle-structure determination in Problem 15.6. Its fixed-point-free involutions are in different constructions. The present claim gives the exact fixed-point law of alpha, a strict finite-size variance excess for rectangular bands with both dimensions >1, and its joint two-side-length Poisson limit. Searches by exact object, transversals, enumeration, and Poisson fixed-point aliases did not identify a dominating result. An unindexed equivalent combinatorial law is a residual risk.
residual_risks: An unindexed complete-mapping or random-grid-permutation study could state an equivalent distribution under different terminology.
The asymptotic is proved only as min(a,b) grows, not uniformly down to fixed side length.

value.rationale: Problem 15.6 of the 2026 foundational paper asks for cycle structure; the exact probability generating polynomial resolves the full length-one cycle law in a natural all-one Rees matrix family. The positive 1/(ab) variance correction reveals nontrivial finite-grid correlations and the Poisson(1) limit quantifies disappearance of this dependence as both dimensions grow. It is not a textbook existence criterion or merely a small finite census.
